choices.text: Guard the stores and move supplies

outcomes.text: You guard the stores and help move loads into a protected yard.

choices.text: Volunteer for the exposed post (risk of death)

outcomes.text: You return from the post with a damaged shield and a clearer understanding of the unit's movements.
A spear strikes your abdomen during the assignment. Blood loss from the wound proves fatal.

events.title: The loads and the equipment
events.text: The unit checks a storehouse and compares its equipment list with the incoming loads. The names at the head of the orders may change; every missing item still has to be explained.

events.title: A passage to Athens
events.text: A returning trader offers to arrange a passage to Athens and a place to stay with readers there. Aristotle is teaching at the Lyceum. Taking the journey would mean a season away from your household; a place in a discussion is not promised.

choices.text: Stay with your household and local teacher

outcomes.text: You ask for a copied argument instead and keep your work near home. This time you do not travel to Athens.

choices.text: Pay 30 drachmas for the round trip to Athens

outcomes.text: In Athens, a reader brings you into a discussion at the Lyceum. Aristotle asks the group to distinguish what a thing is from why it changes. You return to Egypt with a checked set of notes and a question your own teacher cannot dismiss.

The passage reaches Athens late, and the promised introduction does not materialize. Other readers help you examine an argument before you return to Egypt. You have made the journey, but have not heard Aristotle himself.

events.title: Supplies for the king's party
events.text: Alexander's party is inspecting the Egyptian coast. An officer needs local hands to check boat loads and clear a landing. Helping could put you near the king, but a paid task is not an introduction to him.

choices.text: Keep to your existing work

outcomes.text: You leave the officer to find other hands. The party's plans reach you through the people who took the work.

choices.text: Check the loads and help prepare the landing

outcomes.text: You count the loads, clear the landing and receive the agreed payment. The officer keeps your name with the supply account; the work becomes part of the preparations around the new city.

choices.text: Take the work and ask to present the checked account

outcomes.text: After the loads are checked, an officer calls you forward with the account. Alexander asks whether boats can use the landing in a contrary wind. You answer from the shore you know. The exchange is brief; afterward you return to the workers and collect your pay.
The officer accepts the account and pays you, but the king's party moves on before you are called. Your work is recorded; you have not spoken to Alexander.

events.title: The line that the sketch cannot prove
events.text: A reader connected with Euclid's teaching brings you a geometrical construction. A neat drawing will not answer the question: you must explain why the steps hold. Ten drachmas would cover materials and time in the working circle.

choices.text: Keep to the calculations you already use

outcomes.text: You return the construction and finish the accounts waiting on your own table.

choices.text: Pay 10 drachmas and work through the demonstration

outcomes.text: In the teaching circle, Euclid stops at the step you thought was obvious. You rebuild it from the agreed definitions and earlier results. When the demonstration is accepted, you take home a corrected copy whose margin records the point you had to prove.

The readers find a step your explanation does not justify. You leave with a correction to work through, rather than an accepted demonstration. The fee and the failed attempt have still bought a clearer question.

events.title: The convoy musters
events.text: Carts of grain stand loaded at the granary gate. Whoever leads them is answerable for every measure that reaches the army, and for every measure that does not.

choices.text: Set out as you are

outcomes.text: You check the loads once and take the road.

choices.text: Buy extra provisions first (60 dr)

outcomes.text: You pay for extra bread, water skins and spare harness before you leave.

choices.text: Ask someone you trust to ride along

outcomes.text: A friend agrees to ride beside the carts and keep watch.

choices.text: Buy provisions and ask a friend to ride along (60 dr)

outcomes.text: You pay for extra provisions, and a friend rides beside the carts.

choices.text: Decline the convoy

outcomes.text: You hand the carts back. The grain stays where it was, and people remember who would not go.

events.title: On the supply road
events.text: Two days out, the road narrows between dunes and broken walls. How you take the next stretch decides how much grain reaches the army.

choices.text: Push straight through

outcomes.text: The carts roll through without trouble.

weightModifiers.reason: Warfare training
Good health
Dangerous road
Uneasy road

outcomes.text: Raiders cut loose two carts before you drive them off.
An ambush in a narrow cut scatters the carts. You are hurt, and much of the grain is gone.

weightModifiers.reason: Dangerous road
Uneasy road
Warfare training
Good health

choices.text: Take the long road (slower; some grain spoils)

outcomes.text: The long road is slow and some grain spoils in the heat, but no one troubles you.

weightModifiers.reason: Careful reckoning of supplies

outcomes.text: Even on the long road, raiders find the carts at a well.

weightModifiers.reason: Dangerous road
Warfare training

choices.text: Close ranks and guard the cargo

outcomes.text: You close the carts into a ring each night. Nothing is taken.

weightModifiers.reason: Seasoned in warfare
Good health

outcomes.text: You fight off a night raid and lose one cart, but take a wound that festers.

weightModifiers.reason: Good health

outcomes.text: Too many raiders come at once. Your leg is broken in the struggle and much of the grain is lost.

weightModifiers.reason: Dangerous road
Seasoned in warfare

choices.text: Lead the escort through the danger

outcomes.text: You lead the escort through the worst of the road and every cart arrives. Dion enters the convoy in the unit's record with your name at its head.

weightModifiers.reason: Seasoned in warfare
Good health

outcomes.text: You hold the escort together through a hard fight. A few carts are lost and you are wounded, but Dion records that the convoy came through under your lead.
The escort breaks under a heavy attack. Your leg is broken and half the grain is lost.

weightModifiers.reason: Seasoned in warfare

choices.text: Leave part of the cargo behind to get away

outcomes.text: You cut loose the slowest carts and the rest get away.

events.title: Neighbours at the harvest
events.text: Neighbours who know what you have done for the village come with sickles and donkeys to help bring in your harvest.

choices.text: Accept their help and feed them at the harvest table

outcomes.text: With more hands the grain is cut before it can shed. Next harvest should come in fuller, and the evening meal is loud.

choices.text: Thank them and bring the harvest in yourselves

outcomes.text: You send them home with thanks and work the field yourselves from dawn to dark.

events.title: A boundary dispute
events.text: Two neighbouring families quarrel over where one plot ends after the flood moved the markers. Both ask you to decide.

choices.text: Hear both sides at the threshing floor

outcomes.text: You pace the field with both families and set new markers. Both grumble, and both accept it.

choices.text: Send them to the village scribe

outcomes.text: You say it is not your place. The families go to the scribe, and some neighbours think less of you for it.

events.title: A steward from the revenue office
events.text: A steward from Cleomenes' revenue office stops at your door. He has heard of the work you paid for and wants an honest account of the district's harvest.

choices.text: Report the district's harvest for his fee

outcomes.text: You walk the steward through the fields and the stores. He pays you 60 drachmas for the report.

choices.text: Ask him to go easy on the village's grain

outcomes.text: The steward promises nothing, but your neighbours hear that you spoke for them.

events.title: A grain contract
events.text: A townsperson offers to buy grain from your store at a stated price per measure, paid in drachmas on the spot.

choices.text: Sell the grain at the offered price

outcomes.text: You give your answer and the terms are settled.

choices.text: Keep your grain

outcomes.text: You send word that you will not take it.

events.title: Seed grain on credit
events.text: A townsperson offers you grain now, to be paid for later. The price is added to your household debt.

choices.text: Take the grain on credit

outcomes.text: You give your answer and the terms are settled.

choices.text: Do without the credit

outcomes.text: You send word that you will not take it.

events.title: A convoy job
events.text: A townsperson offers you pay in drachmas to guard a grain convoy on the road. Only a serving soldier can take it.

choices.text: Take the convoy job

outcomes.text: You give your answer and the terms are settled.

choices.text: Turn the job down

outcomes.text: You send word that you will not take it.

events.title: A goods deal
events.text: The merchant offers you trade goods at a stated price per unit, paid in drachmas.

choices.text: Buy the goods at the offered price

outcomes.text: You give your answer and the terms are settled.

choices.text: Keep your drachmas

outcomes.text: You send word that you will not take it.

events.title: The flood fails
events.text: The Nile stays low through the flood season and the water never reaches the upper fields. The neighbouring farm expects a poor harvest, and the merchant's grain prices are already rising. Your household must decide how to get through the year.

choices.text: Cut every portion and keep the seed grain for sowing

outcomes.text: Everyone eats less this year, but the seed grain stays in its jars and the whole plot is sown when the water allows.

choices.text: Sell a piece of silver to raise money for grain

outcomes.text: A dealer pays 50 drachmas for your silver. The money will buy grain if the store runs short.

effect.cause: sold to buy grain in the flood year

choices.text: Sell two bolts of linen to raise money for grain

outcomes.text: A dealer pays 40 drachmas for the linen. The money will buy grain if the store runs short.

effect.cause: sold to buy grain in the flood year

choices.text: Share 100 measures of grain with neighbours who have none

outcomes.text: You carry baskets of grain to the neighbours whose stores are empty. Your own store is smaller, but the district remembers who helped.

events.title: The levy comes to the district
events.text: Army officers arrive to raise men and supplies. Every household with someone fit to serve is listed, and the officers will also take provisions or a substitute's fee. Whoever goes, their labour leaves the family plot.

choices.text: Stay on the farm and keep working the plot

outcomes.text: You keep working the plot. The officer notes your name, and some neighbours mutter that others went in your place.

choices.text: Enlist as a soldier

outcomes.text: You report to the muster and are enrolled as a soldier. Your labour leaves the family plot while you serve.

choices.text: Report to the muster for drill

outcomes.text: The officer finds you too raw for the ranks and sets you to drill with the recruits for a season. You come home knowing the basics.

choices.text: Send 150 measures of grain to the muster

outcomes.text: Your household loads grain onto a cart for the muster. The officer records the gift against your name.

effect.cause: provisions sent to the army muster

choices.text: Pay the 60-drachma substitute fee

outcomes.text: The officer takes the fee and enters a hired man in your place. Your household keeps its labour on the plot.

events.title: Not every grain belongs in the seed basket
events.text: A neighbour brings a small sample of next season's grain. Some kernels are damaged. The neighbour asks which differences you would examine before choosing seed.

choices.text: Compare the sound and damaged kernels

outcomes.text: You separate the sound kernels from the damaged ones and explain which differences you can observe. The grower asks you to compare the next crop with these first impressions.

choices.text: Ask an experienced grower to explain their choices

outcomes.text: The grower describes how they choose seed and where they have been wrong before. You leave with better questions for the next fieldwork year.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your household duties.

events.title: Two households want the same water turn
events.text: Neighbours compare the channel timetable before the next growing season. One family wants an earlier turn; another says that would leave its lower plot dry. They ask you to compare the needs before the timetable is agreed.

choices.text: Compare plot levels and the proposed timetable

outcomes.text: You mark where the water has to travel and revise the timetable with both households. Both families can now see why the same timetable affects their plots differently.

choices.text: Hear both families before proposing a compromise

outcomes.text: You make the competing needs explicit and ask each family to name a workable concession. The argument ends more calmly, without a promise of extra water.

choices.text: Back your relatives before checking the other plot

outcomes.text: Your relatives welcome the support, but the other household says you have not heard its case. The discussion teaches you how quickly a timetable becomes a dispute.

events.title: The plan looks better than the fields
events.text: Your draft of an integrated cultivation plan assumes every workday will go smoothly. A fellow grower asks what happens if illness or a broken tool takes a week out of the season.

choices.text: Revise the plan around available labour

outcomes.text: You remove an ambitious task and make the labour shortfall visible in the estimates. The revised plan leaves room for a delay instead of promising more work than the household can do.

choices.text: Ask another household to review the weakest assumption

outcomes.text: They identify a maintenance task you had treated as free. You correct the explanation and acknowledge their contribution.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the plan you can currently support.

events.title: Seed sacks and supper sacks
events.text: Two similar sacks have been marked for different purposes. A child asks why grain kept for sowing should not be counted twice when the household plans its meals.

choices.text: Explain the separate seed and food counts

outcomes.text: You lay out the two purposes and check the written totals. The household can now distinguish food already promised to meals from grain intended for sowing.

choices.text: Teach the household a clearer labelling method

outcomes.text: You agree on marks that everyone can distinguish and ask each person to explain them back. The labels make a future mistake less likely.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the household's current reserve arrangements.

events.title: The store count is short
events.text: The figures in a stock note do not match a neighbour's recollection. The difference could be a counting error or an unrecorded withdrawal; an accusation would travel faster than either explanation.

choices.text: Recount the entries before blaming anyone

outcomes.text: You find which line needs checking and separate the observed count from an assumption about theft. The household agrees to check that entry together before making an accusation.

choices.text: Ask everyone who used the store to explain the note

outcomes.text: The conversation is awkward, but the household agrees that uncertainty should be recorded before blame. The household agrees to keep the uncertain entry visible while the count is checked.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your existing reserve plan.

events.title: A shortage that has not happened yet
events.text: Before a difficult season, neighbours ask you to explain your reserve plan under a smaller harvest. They want to know which purchases are affordable and which depend on grain nobody actually owns.

choices.text: Recalculate the plan using only existing reserves and cash

outcomes.text: You distinguish a possible purchase from grain already in store and identify the point at which the plan would fail. You can now point to the weak place in the plan before a poor harvest exposes it.

choices.text: Explain the limits openly to the neighbours

outcomes.text: You make no promise that every loss can be covered. The households agree to compare their actual positions after the next settlement.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the commitments already made.

events.title: The useful piece between two cuts
events.text: At a textile bench, two ways of laying out a sample pattern leave different offcuts. The maker invites you to explain the measurements before any cloth is committed to an order.

choices.text: Mark the sample and compare its dimensions

outcomes.text: You discover that a tidy-looking arrangement can still give the wrong size. The maker turns the sample around and asks you to check the same measurement from the other edge.

choices.text: Ask the maker why one offcut is still useful

outcomes.text: They show where a small piece can serve a different purpose. You learn to describe the material honestly rather than treating every scrap as waste.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your current apprenticeship.

events.title: The garment and the customer's measure
events.text: A customer and a maker disagree about which measurements were agreed. You are asked to read the old note, whose shortest line admits two different interpretations.

choices.text: Compare the written measure with the sample

outcomes.text: You identify the ambiguous line and suggest a clearer specification for the next fitting. The customer and maker agree to write down that measure before another fitting.

choices.text: Help both sides agree how the next fitting will be checked

outcomes.text: You keep the discussion about the agreed measure rather than personal pride. Both sides leave with a clearer question to put to the inspector.

choices.text: Defend the maker's reading without offering a new fitting

outcomes.text: You argue the written wording firmly. The customer leaves unconvinced, and the disagreement becomes harder to settle.

events.title: Four garments, one accepted standard
events.text: A patron's draft brief calls four ceremonial garments 'fine' without defining the workmanship. Before a masterwork assessment can begin, the specification must say what an inspector can actually accept.

choices.text: Write a checkable standard for fit and finish

outcomes.text: You separate the patron's preferences from the inspection criteria. The inspector can now say what would make the set acceptable, and the patron knows what has been promised.

choices.text: Ask the patron to explain the intended use

outcomes.text: The conversation reveals which parts need to survive repeated wear and which are decorative. You can now discuss the order without promising an impossible finish.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the orders you have already accepted.

events.title: Clay that behaves differently overnight
events.text: Two small clay samples look alike at first, but one has begun to crack. A potter asks you to describe the difference before offering an explanation.

choices.text: Compare moisture, thickness and the visible cracks

outcomes.text: You distinguish what you can see from a guess about the cause. The potter sets the samples aside so their changes can be compared again tomorrow.

choices.text: Ask how the potter records a failed trial

outcomes.text: They show why a failed sample is useful only when its conditions were recorded. You agree to keep a clearer note on your next real work year.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your existing workshop tasks.

events.title: One side of the kiln runs hotter
events.text: A firing note records an uneven result. The discussion turns to the placement of vessels and the path of the draft, rather than a promise that more fuel always makes better pottery.

choices.text: Compare positions in the kiln with the reported results

outcomes.text: You find which comparison would make the next firing more informative. The next loading plan now names which positions to compare and where the draft must be watched.

choices.text: Ask the crew to explain their loading choices

outcomes.text: You hear why one arrangement was chosen and where the crew was uncertain. Their practical account makes your next question more precise.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the firing method you can currently support.

events.title: A set must match in use
events.text: A buyer asks for vessels that work together, not merely pieces that look impressive alone. The draft order has to explain the acceptable capacity, finish and variation before a master assessment starts.

choices.text: Define the matching standard in measurable terms

outcomes.text: You turn a vague request into dimensions and an inspection question. The buyer points out which differences would make a piece awkward to use, and you amend the brief.

choices.text: Discuss how the set will be carried and used

outcomes.text: The buyer explains which variation matters in daily handling. You add the handling requirement to the brief rather than leaving it to guesswork.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the commissions already on your bench.

events.title: The likeness changes when you move
events.text: A model's profile looks different from the front view. A sculptor asks you which features belong to the person and which belong to the viewpoint.

choices.text: Compare the views before changing the model

outcomes.text: You describe the relationship between the views and avoid correcting one by guessing at the other. The sculptor asks you to keep both views beside the model as you work.

choices.text: Ask the sitter what feels wrong about the likeness

outcomes.text: Their answer makes you notice an expression you had ignored. Listening becomes part of the work rather than a substitute for making it.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your current making exercises.

events.title: The line inside the stone
events.text: A sketch of a stone figure crosses a visible vein. The maker asks whether the plan should be changed before the next piece of stone is bought and cut.

choices.text: Revise the plan around the observed weakness

outcomes.text: You change the proposed load and compare what the alteration does to the figure. The cutter marks the risky line on the sketch and explains where a change would be safer.

choices.text: Ask a more experienced cutter to review the risk

outcomes.text: They explain which uncertainty can be inspected and which would remain after the cut. You acknowledge the advice in your working note.

choices.text: Test the rough sample without following the cutter's advice

outcomes.text: A sharp edge catches your hand before the test tells you anything useful. You stop and compare the sample with the sketch more carefully.

events.title: A public relief has several audiences
events.text: A proposed public relief has to be legible to people who stand close to it and people who pass at a distance. The patron's description says little about either view.

choices.text: Compare scale, viewing distance and the proposed relief

outcomes.text: You identify what a large-work plan must show before anyone commits materials. The new sketch makes the distant view clearer without losing the details intended for a close observer.

choices.text: Listen to the people who will use the space

outcomes.text: Their questions expose a feature the patron had overlooked. You revise the brief while making clear who contributed the observation.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the work already promised.

events.title: Two accounts of the same event
events.text: Two readers describe the same incident differently. One account is more elegant; the other names observations that could be checked. A teacher asks which claim you would investigate first.

choices.text: Separate the claims and list what could be checked

outcomes.text: You distinguish testimony, inference and a missing observation. You leave with a short list of observations that could distinguish the two accounts.

choices.text: Ask both readers how they reached their conclusion

outcomes.text: Each has to expose an assumption they had left unstated. You learn to ask a focused question without pretending the dispute is settled.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the questions already under study.

events.title: The observation that does not fit
events.text: A colleague points to a result that sits badly with your preferred explanation. Removing it would make the account easier to present, but would also hide the question a new test should answer.

choices.text: Keep the observation and explain the discrepancy

outcomes.text: You distinguish a difficult result from a useless one and describe a possible comparison. The difficult result becomes a question to investigate instead of a line to conceal.

choices.text: Ask another reader to check the observation first

outcomes.text: You preserve the uncertain result and invite a check of the procedure. The reader agrees to check the procedure and compare their notes with yours.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your current inquiry.

events.title: Who can reproduce the inquiry?
events.text: Before an original inquiry is assessed, a fellow reader asks whether someone else could follow the record, identify the sources and understand the limits of the result.

choices.text: Make the method and limitations explicit

outcomes.text: You improve the account and identify which earlier observations support it. The reader can now follow where the account is secure and where its conclusion remains uncertain.

choices.text: Invite the contributors to check how their work is credited

outcomes.text: They correct an omission in the working record. You make the contribution visible and preserve the distinction between your result and theirs.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the material that is already ready for review.

events.title: The quieter voice at the hearing
events.text: At a small neighbourhood discussion, confident speakers interrupt someone who has brought a relevant observation. The chair asks how you would make the exchange useful.

choices.text: Ask for the observation before the next speech

outcomes.text: The discussion gains a detail that had been missing. The chair gives the quieter speaker time to explain how they know it.

choices.text: Summarise the points of agreement and disagreement

outcomes.text: The participants can see where they differ rather than arguing past one another. Both sides correct the summary, and the disagreement becomes more precise.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your present obligations.

events.title: Two receipts, one public payment
events.text: A copy of a district receipt gives a different amount from the original. The officials want a quick explanation, while the households want the figures checked before anyone is accused.

choices.text: Trace the entry back to the original receipt

outcomes.text: You identify the line that needs reconciliation and explain the uncertainty plainly. You show the officials exactly which entry must be checked before the accounts can be explained.

choices.text: Explain why the discrepancy must remain visible until checked

outcomes.text: The delay is unpopular, but people understand what is known and what is still uncertain. You resist giving an unsupported answer.

choices.text: Give the officials a quick answer before checking the original

outcomes.text: The answer sounds confident until someone produces a conflicting note. You learn how to hold an audience, but lose trust by speaking beyond the evidence.

events.title: The cost falls on a different household
events.text: A district proposal looks affordable in total, but a neighbour points out that its cost falls unevenly. Before a final assessment, the policy record needs to show who gains, who pays and what happened after implementation.

choices.text: Compare the household costs with the expected benefit

outcomes.text: You revise the explanation to distinguish a total from its distribution. You add the uneven burden to the discussion instead of hiding it inside a favourable total.

choices.text: Hear the affected households before defending the proposal

outcomes.text: They identify a cost the first account had missed. You acknowledge it and explain the remaining trade-off without promising an outcome nobody can guarantee.

choices.text: Defend the favourable total and dismiss the distribution

outcomes.text: You make a forceful speech, but the households carrying the cost feel unheard. They ask why their loss has disappeared inside your total.

events.title: The baskets do not hold the same amount
events.text: Two traders quote the same price for baskets of different sizes. A buyer asks which offer is cheaper once the measure, not just the spoken number, is compared.

choices.text: Compare price per equal measure

outcomes.text: You show why the smaller spoken price need not be the cheaper purchase. The buyer asks for both offers in the same measure before choosing.

choices.text: Ask each trader to state their measure clearly

outcomes.text: Both quotes become easier to compare, and the buyer can make an informed choice. The clearer terms reduce the room for a later dispute.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to your current trade.

events.title: A cheap quote with an uncertain delivery
events.text: A supplier's low quote omits the delivery date and who bears a transport loss. The plan should identify those terms before goods or money are committed.

choices.text: Compare the full delivered cost and the missing terms

outcomes.text: You separate the attractive headline price from the costs the quote leaves open. You write the unanswered questions beside the price rather than assuming them away.

choices.text: Ask the supplier to state the obligations on both sides

outcomes.text: The discussion clarifies where each party's responsibility would begin and end. The quote is less impressive at first glance, but its obligations are easier to understand.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the supply arrangements you can presently honour.

events.title: The margin exists only on paper
events.text: A trading-house plan counts a customer's expected payment as if the cash were already in hand. A reviewer asks whether the next purchase could still be paid for if the customer were late.

choices.text: Separate cash, expected receipts and committed costs

outcomes.text: You expose the gap between profit on paper and money available to use. The reviewer can now see which commitment the available cash will actually cover.

choices.text: Explain the uncertainty before agreeing to the next order

outcomes.text: The customer may dislike the caution, but both parties understand what can actually be promised. You leave the next order open until both parties can make a promise they can keep.

choices.text: Keep to your current work

outcomes.text: You leave the discussion and return to the commitments already funded.

events.title: What makes useful work for Alexander the Great?
events.text: Enter through campaign service while Alexander is in Egypt. Logistics, command and a completed strategic operation matter; an age-28 General appointment is not an entry requirement. The working circle asks you to retain the reasons, costs and revisions behind your contribution, rather than rely on the prestige of the name.

choices.text: Keep a clear record and invite criticism

outcomes.text: You improve the record and identify the next work that needs doing. The clearer notes give the next season of work a useful starting point.

choices.text: Ask the other workers to compare their experience

outcomes.text: Comparing experience builds trust and exposes a point worth checking in your next actual work year.

events.title: Credit and responsibility in Alexander the Great's tradition
events.text: Your completed contributions now attract attention. A collaborator asks which claims belong to the historical tradition, which results you actually delivered, and which uncertainties remain. A famous name does not settle those questions.

choices.text: Credit the workers and state the limits of the evidence

outcomes.text: The record distinguishes your completed work from earlier achievements and uncertain claims. The collaborators can now see which result rests on which season of work.

choices.text: Recheck the result before presenting it

outcomes.text: You identify a weak claim and plan a more careful check. You leave a specific question for the next review.

events.title: What makes useful work for Aristotle?
events.text: Start with argument and observation at the Lyceum, then build reviewed inquiry and teaching. Later work continues through the Aristotelian school and makes no claim of a dead teacher's personal endorsement. The working circle asks you to retain the reasons, costs and revisions behind your contribution, rather than rely on the prestige of the name.

choices.text: Keep a clear record and invite criticism

outcomes.text: You improve the record and identify the next work that needs doing. The clearer notes give the next season of work a useful starting point.

choices.text: Ask the other workers to compare their experience

outcomes.text: Comparing experience builds trust and exposes a point worth checking in your next actual work year.

events.title: What makes useful work for Euclid?
events.text: Join the geometrical tradition associated with the Elements around 300 BCE. The path rewards justified constructions and a coherent deductive collection, without inventing a Museum appointment or a precise death date. The working circle asks you to retain the reasons, costs and revisions behind your contribution, rather than rely on the prestige of the name.

endings.title: Death in infancy
endings.text: You die before your first birthday. Your household arranges your funeral.

endings.title: Death in childhood
endings.text: You die during childhood. Your household arranges your funeral.

endings.title: Death in adulthood
endings.text: You die as an adult. Your household arranges your funeral and deals with your unfinished work.

endings.title: Death in later life
endings.text: You die in later life. Your household arranges your funeral and sorts your belongings.

endings.title: Record complete
endings.text: The record stops at age 100. This is the end of the simulation record, not a recorded death.

endings.title: Killed by a collector
endings.text: A collector stabs you during a confrontation over the unpaid loan. The chest wound proves fatal.

sources.title: Strabo, Geography 17.1.3–10: the Nile and Alexandria
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; H. L. Jones, Loeb translation (1932)
sources.period: Augustan-era account of Egypt and Alexandria, referring also to earlier Ptolemaic history
sources.geography: Alexandria and the Nile valley
sources.summary: Describes Alexandria's harbors, Pharos, streets and royal district, and the importance of Nile inundation, canals and agricultural management.
sources.limitations: Elite literary testimony with Roman imperial sympathies. Descriptive claims and reported numbers are not a population survey, an exact city map or annual household probabilities.

sources.title: Bellum Alexandrinum 1–33: the Alexandrian War
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; Loeb translation (1955)
sources.period: Events of 48–47 BCE; authorship traditionally associated with the Caesarian corpus
sources.geography: Alexandria and the Nile Delta
sources.summary: Narrates fighting, barricades, harbor operations and disruption of Caesar's water supply during the Alexandrian War.
sources.limitations: A partisan Roman military narrative with prejudicial descriptions of Alexandrians. It supports a war setting, not invented civilian experiences, precise casualty odds or a claim that the entire Library was destroyed.

sources.title: Chronological Tables for Caesar's Wars (58–45 BCE)
sources.publisher: John T. Ramsey and Kurt A. Raaflaub, Histos 11 (2017); journal page published online 2018
sources.period: 58–45 BCE, including the Alexandrian War of 48–47 BCE
sources.geography: Roman campaigns including Alexandria and Egypt
sources.summary: Reconstructs the sequence of Caesar's campaigns and separates Roman civil-calendar dates from reconstructed Julian dates.
sources.limitations: A scholarly chronology reconstructed from ancient testimony. Day-level dates may be disputed; the game uses year-level anchors and does not reproduce whole tables.

sources.title: Ptolemaic Period
sources.publisher: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities
sources.period: 332–30 BCE; Actium in 31 BCE and the end of Ptolemaic rule in 30 BCE
sources.geography: Egypt, with Alexandria as capital
sources.summary: Provides a heritage-authority overview of Ptolemaic Egypt and the transition following the defeat at Actium.
sources.limitations: A broad public-history overview, not a detailed social dataset. Use the year-level chronology without treating its compressed narrative as proof of every personal consequence.

sources.title: Augustus, Res Gestae, especially section 27
sources.publisher: Livius.org; F. W. Shipley translation from LacusCurtius
sources.period: Augustus's retrospective inscription, completed near the end of his reign in 14 CE
sources.geography: Roman Empire; section 27 concerns annexation of Egypt
sources.summary: Augustus claims to have added Egypt to Roman rule. The inscription offers a contemporary imperial voice for the political transition.
sources.limitations: Self-promotional imperial testimony. It does not describe the response of all Egyptians and must be paired with independent chronology and local evidence.

sources.title: Alexandrian Documents from the Reign of Augustus
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, Department of Classics, University of Cincinnati
sources.period: Augustan Alexandria, especially 13 BCE; individual texts and later additions have their own dates
sources.geography: Documents issued in Alexandria, many recovered from reused cartonnage at Abusir el-Melek
sources.summary: Provides scholarly English translations of Alexandrian contracts, letters, petitions and association records, with document identifiers and links to the underlying Greek texts.
sources.limitations: The surviving archive is selective, not representative of every household. Early Roman material is comparative evidence for earlier Ptolemaic years; use each document's actual date.

sources.title: BGU 4.1125.1–15: apprenticeship contract for a musician
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: March/April 13 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Records training in flute playing, the term of apprenticeship, provision of food and clothing, and examination by fellow practitioners.
sources.limitations: The apprentice is enslaved, and this is a specific musical contract. It is evidence for organized training, not universal schooling or the terms of a free child's scribal apprenticeship.

sources.title: BGU 4.1058: wetnursing contract
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: 30 March 13 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Documents paid nursing, infant care and a clause anticipating the possibility of a child's death.
sources.limitations: Both nurse and infant are enslaved in this contract. Its clauses show contemporary concerns; they do not estimate infant mortality or demonstrate that every household employed a wet nurse.

sources.title: BGU 4.1052.1–34: marriage contract
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: 15 April 13 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Records an agreement for a shared life, a dowry and economic and marital obligations.
sources.limitations: One Greek-language legal agreement, with particular status and guardianship conventions. Its terms are not universal Egyptian marriage rules or an observed marriage-age distribution.

sources.title: BGU 4.1141: private letter
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: After 9 April 13 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Preserves correspondence concerning friendship, accusations, work, wages and interpersonal obligations.
sources.limitations: A fragmentary and sometimes difficult personal letter, embedded in unequal relationships. It supports written communication as a theme, not the fictional character's letter or a literacy rate.

sources.title: BGU 4.1117: lease contract for a bakery
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: April/May 13 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria, Beta quarter
sources.summary: Describes a bakery lease, equipment, rent, repairs and responsibility for taxes, illustrating workshop livelihoods and contractual obligations.
sources.limitations: A single bakery agreement. Monetary amounts and conditions cannot be generalized to all trades or converted directly into the game's abstract wealth score.

sources.title: BGU 4.1151.1–18: partial payment of an inheritance
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: 12 April 13 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Records an agreement concerning the partial payment of an inheritance, supporting a narrative theme of property and obligations between generations.
sources.limitations: A particular legal settlement. It supplies neither a representative inheritance amount nor evidence that all older people held transferable property.

sources.title: Education and Apprenticeship
sources.publisher: Nikolaos Lazaridis (2010), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
sources.period: Survey across ancient Egyptian periods, including Ptolemaic and Roman bilingual education
sources.geography: Ancient Egypt; not exclusively Alexandria
sources.summary: Reviews training for scribes and specialist crafts, educational exercises and restricted access to formal schooling.
sources.limitations: A long-period synthesis with uneven evidence. It cannot supply exact Alexandrian enrolment or literacy probabilities, and does not justify giving every child formal schooling.

sources.title: Funerary Rituals (Ptolemaic and Roman Periods)
sources.publisher: Christina Riggs (2010), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology; University of East Anglia repository
sources.period: Ptolemaic and Roman periods
sources.geography: Egypt; evidence includes Akhmim, Thebes, Tuna el-Gebel and other communities
sources.summary: Surveys burial, commemoration, mourning and funerary associations, including arrangements for members to contribute to funeral costs.
sources.limitations: Rites varied with community, status, resources and religion. Elite mummification evidence is not a universal Alexandrian funeral script; use broad remembrance themes carefully.

sources.title: The abuse of aged parents in the ancient Roman world
sources.publisher: Tim Parkin, Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies 66(2), 41–50; online 2024
sources.period: Roman world with Ptolemaic Egyptian petitions of 225 and 221 BCE among the comparative cases
sources.geography: Roman Mediterranean and the Arsinoite nome in Egypt
sources.summary: Examines duties, dependence and care between generations, including papyrus petitions by older parents.
sources.limitations: Sparse, often one-sided dispute evidence from varied times and places. It does not establish rates of neglect or a uniform old-age household arrangement in Alexandria.

sources.title: Volcanic suppression of Nile summer flooding triggers revolt and constrains interstate conflict in ancient Egypt
sources.publisher: Joseph G. Manning and colleagues (2017), Nature Communications 8, 900; author copy at UC Berkeley
sources.period: Ptolemaic Egypt, 305–30 BCE, with later Nilometer measurements used for comparison
sources.geography: Nile basin and Egypt; papyrus survival particularly strong in the Fayyum
sources.summary: Combines environmental reconstructions and ancient writings to examine Nile flood variability, agricultural vulnerability and social stress.
sources.limitations: Ancient flood indications are intermittent and may have dating uncertainty. The continuous Nilometer series begins in 622 CE; this is not a precise annual Alexandrian food-price or famine-risk dataset.

sources.title: Roman Model Life Table (Coale–Demeny Female West Level 3)
sources.publisher: Columbia University / W. V. Harris teaching resources
sources.period: Comparative Roman demographic model; not an observed Ptolemaic cohort
sources.geography: Roman comparison model; not an Alexandria-specific dataset
sources.summary: Provides age-band mortality, survivorship and remaining life expectancy for a model population with life expectancy at birth of 25 years.
sources.limitations: A female model life table, not measured male Alexandrian rates. Converting interval death probabilities into annual hazards assumes within-band timing. Age at death is simulated, not a historical prediction.

sources.title: Quantifying antiquity
sources.publisher: Roger S. Bagnall, Columbia University
sources.period: Contrasts Roman Egyptian census evidence with Hellenistic Egyptian household lists
sources.geography: Egypt, with wider methodological comparisons
sources.summary: Explains the promise and limits of ancient demographic evidence, including why Hellenistic household lists without ages cannot yield life expectancy.
sources.limitations: A methodological essay rather than a downloadable life table. It explicitly cautions against combining Roman and Hellenistic evidence without careful analysis.

sources.title: Life Expectancy
sources.publisher: Sonia Zakrzewski (2015), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
sources.period: Long-period review of ancient Egyptian demographic evidence, including Roman model tables
sources.geography: Egypt; evidence from varied populations and sites
sources.summary: Explains demographic methods and biases. Table 1 reproduces a model life table for Roman Egyptian females after Bagnall and Frier (1994), with life expectancy at birth of 22.5 years.
sources.limitations: A later-period female model inferred using census returns and Coale–Demeny West, not observed mortality for a male in Ptolemaic Alexandria. Annual interpolation and the final age-band policy are additional game assumptions; cause-of-death rates are not supplied.

sources.title: Zodiaque de Dendéra (E 13482)
sources.publisher: Musée du Louvre, Egyptian Antiquities collection
sources.period: 50 BCE; catalogue dates the relief to June–August
sources.geography: Hathor temple, Dendera, Upper Egypt
sources.summary: Catalogues a sandstone ceiling relief with zodiacal signs, decans and constellations, providing a contemporary example of Egyptian astral imagery.
sources.limitations: A temple object from Dendera, not an Alexandrian teaching manual. It supplies neither access probabilities nor evidence that astrological predictions were reliable.

sources.title: Alexandrian terracottas
sources.publisher: Vatican Museums, Gregorian Egyptian Museum
sources.period: Ptolemaic and Roman periods
sources.geography: Alexandria; collection objects have varied acquisition histories
sources.summary: Describes Alexandrian figurative terracottas, including mould-made examples and a range of decorative and religious subjects.
sources.limitations: The collection spans multiple periods and some objects entered through the antiquities market. It does not measure workshop employment, wages or apprenticeship access.

sources.title: Statuette of an ancestral king (2003.154)
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.period: Late Period–Early Ptolemaic Period, 380–246 BCE
sources.geography: Egypt; exact workshop not established in this catalogue entry
sources.summary: Documents a carved wooden ritual figure associated with temple equipment, illustrating skilled Egyptian wood carving.
sources.limitations: Earlier than the player's lifetime and not specifically Alexandrian. The object's interpretation is debated; it does not establish a universal carving curriculum or job ladder.

sources.title: An enigmatic early horoscope: BKT X 29 (P. 11831)
sources.publisher: Berlin Papyrus Database, Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection; Marius Gerhardt, Andreas Winkler and Michael Zellmann-Rohrer
sources.period: Late Ptolemaic or early Roman handwriting; astronomical reconstruction best fits 5 June 29 BCE
sources.geography: Egypt; no Alexandrian workshop identified
sources.summary: Examines a Greek horoscope listing astral positions, abbreviations, the ascendant and midheaven, with possible professional or client use.
sources.limitations: The papyrus lacks a personal name and explicit date, and its solar position conflicts with the proposed reconstruction. Its use is uncertain, and no accompanying interpretation survives.

sources.title: Plutarch, Life of Antony 80: Areius and Octavian at Alexandria
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb translation
sources.period: Later biography describing the Roman takeover of Alexandria in 30 BCE
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Depicts the philosopher Areius receiving public favour from Octavian and interceding for others, illustrating elite intellectual patronage and political access.
sources.limitations: A retrospective literary account, not an administrative record or promotion dataset. It concerns an exceptional elite figure and does not prove ordinary access to Cleopatra's court.

sources.title: Coins in Egypt: Coins of the Ptolemies
sources.publisher: University College London, Digital Egypt for Universities
sources.period: Ptolemaic Egypt, with an overview of earlier coinage
sources.geography: Egypt
sources.summary: Introduces Ptolemaic coin circulation, drachma denominations, bronze and silver coinage, and debt settlement as part of the economy.
sources.limitations: An overview of money and denominations, not an Alexandrian household budget or price series. It does not support the game's prices, wages, asset valuations, fixed returns or a constant currency standard across Roman rule; these remain disclosed gameplay assumptions.

sources.title: LGPN-Egypt: personal names in Egypt
sources.publisher: University of Oxford, Lexicon of Greek Personal Names
sources.period: Current completed coverage: Lower Egypt and the Fayum from the seventh century BCE to 30 BCE; the wider project extends into Roman Egypt
sources.geography: Egypt, with current database coverage focused on Lower Egypt and the Fayum
sources.summary: Introduces a source-based naming database that records personal names alongside attested occupations, dates, family connections and provenance. It supports a varied Greek-language and Egyptian-rendered naming context for fictional characters.
sources.limitations: The game does not reproduce database individuals or claim that every selected name is attested in Alexandria in 66 BCE. Names are not demographic weights, ethnic labels, gender rules or evidence that an occupation belonged to a particular community. Household profiles and event rewards remain authored fiction.

sources.title: Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 1.81.7: childhood learning and livelihood
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; C. H. Oldfather, Loeb translation (1933)
sources.period: First-century BCE literary account of Egyptian customs
sources.geography: Egypt generally; not an Alexandrian household survey
sources.summary: Describes children learning livelihood skills from fathers and relatives, alongside limited and uneven access to literacy instruction.
sources.limitations: A generalizing literary account without numerical starting ages. It supports learning and work overlapping in childhood, not the game's exact age gates, wage amounts, universal schooling or an identical experience across households.

sources.title: BGU 4.1124: cancellation of a nailsmith's apprenticeship
sources.publisher: University of Cincinnati, Ancient Alexandria documentary translations
sources.period: After June/July 18 BCE, under early Roman rule
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Records Hermaiskos, a son not yet of age, being trained in nailsmithing; cancelling the agreement permits his father to place him with another master.
sources.limitations: The apprentice's numerical age is unstated. The document postdates the cohort's Ptolemaic childhood and does not establish age 12 as a norm, free access to an apprenticeship or the game's pay and skill gains.

sources.title: BGU 4.1151.2: Loan agreement
sources.publisher: University of Cincinnati; Peter van Minnen translation
sources.period: 12 April 13 BCE, early Roman period
sources.geography: Alexandria
sources.summary: Records a money loan with scheduled instalments, default penalties and enforcement claims against debtors and workshop property.
sources.limitations: One early Roman contract, later than the Ptolemaic beginning of the game. Contractual enforcement clauses do not establish how frequently they were exercised or support violent collectors, murder, or the game's loan terms and risks.

sources.title: The Ptolemaic Period (332–30 BCE)
sources.publisher: Brian Muhs (2016); The Ancient Egyptian Economy: 3000–30 BCE, Cambridge University Press; pp. 211–252; DOI 10.1017/CBO9781316286364.008
sources.period: Ptolemaic Egypt, 332–30 BCE; individual examples have earlier dates
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Contracts, witnesses, registration, informal trust and varied exchange networks. Read scope: Relevant full-text sections, especially pp.227–230,236–238,246–247.
sources.limitations: Egypt-wide synthesis with earlier and provincial examples; does not establish exact Alexandrian prices, wages or access rules for this cohort. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Introduction
sources.publisher: Nico Dogaer (2026); Industry, Trade and the State in Ptolemaic Egypt, Cambridge University Press; pp. 1–20; DOI 10.1017/9781009413411.005
sources.period: Ptolemaic Egypt; institutional discussion across the period
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Sector-specific state intervention alongside private activity and local networks. Read scope: Publisher abstract and authorized excerpt pp.1–10; not the full book.
sources.limitations: Institutional framework, not a dossier of one Alexandrian business or proof of unrestricted modern entrepreneurship. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Family Affairs: Guild Regulations and Family Relationships in Roman Egypt
sources.publisher: Philip F. Venticinque (2010); Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies 50(2); pp. 273–294
sources.period: Roman Egypt; near-cohort examples from 14–37 CE and 16 CE, with many later comparisons
sources.geography: Egypt and the wider Mediterranean; see the specific regional limits below
sources.summary: Overlap of household, business, apprenticeship and mutual-support relationships. Read scope: Relevant full-text sections pp.277–283,288–292.
sources.limitations: Chiefly provincial Roman Egypt; cases from43CE,47CE and later are outside the cohort. Earlier comparative cases do not establish Alexandrian guild rules. Characters, accomplishment titles, wages, prices and probabilities in the game are authored fiction.

sources.title: Music and Musicians

sources.title: Strabo, Geography 17.1.6–8: Rhakotis and Alexandria

sources.geography: Egyptian Mediterranean coast, Rhakotis and Alexandria
sources.summary: Describes Rhakotis as a settlement preceding Alexandria, the suitability of the harbor and the tradition of Alexander directing the city's foundation.
sources.limitations: Written centuries after the foundation. Its later urban description is not a map of the coast in 350 BCE. The settlement's extent, inhabitants and individual household experiences are not established by this account.

sources.title: Alexandria, Egypt, before Alexander the Great: A multidisciplinary approach yields rich discoveries
sources.publisher: Jean-Daniel Stanley and colleagues, GSA Today 17(8), 2007; doi:10.1130/GSAT01708A.1

sources.geography: Alexandria's East Harbor and adjacent mainland coast
sources.summary: Archaeological, sedimentary and geochemical indicators support human activity on the coast long before Alexander and a pre-existing settlement beneath the later city.
sources.limitations: The exact location, size and organization of Rhakotis remain uncertain. This evidence does not supply a detailed 350 BCE city plan or demographic rates. The paper uses 332 BCE for Alexandria's foundation; the game adopts the conventional 331 BCE year from its separate chronology source.

sources.title: Egypt in the Ptolemaic Period
sources.publisher: Marsha Hill, Department of Egyptian Art, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2016)
sources.period: Egypt before Alexander and the Ptolemaic period, including 343, 332 and 305 BCE
sources.geography: Egypt and the western Nile Delta
sources.summary: Places Persian reconquest in 343 BCE, Alexander's takeover in 332 BCE and Ptolemy's kingship in 305 BCE. It also describes earlier Greek-Egyptian trade through Delta ports and Naukratis.
sources.limitations: An institutional overview rather than a household history. Political dates do not establish every local response, equal access to professions or the game's numerical rewards. Ptolemy governing after Alexander's death must be distinguished from his later adoption of kingship.

sources.title: The Rise of Macedon and the Conquests of Alexander the Great
sources.publisher: Colette Hemingway and Seán Hemingway, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (2004)

sources.geography: Macedon, Greece, Asia and Egypt
sources.summary: Provides the accession and campaign sequence for Alexander, including his crossing into Asia in 334 BCE and the succession crisis following his death.
sources.limitations: A broad political and art-historical account, not evidence that the fictional player met Alexander. Personal conversations, access to his entourage, recruitment outcomes and civilian consequences are authored situations.

sources.title: Pergamon and the Hellenistic Kingdoms of the Ancient World: chronology
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, exhibition catalogue (2016)

sources.geography: Mediterranean and Hellenistic kingdoms

sources.limitations: A year-level chronology. The game's precise annual ordering is a calendar convention, not a reconstruction of exact foundation ceremonies, building completion dates or individual participation.

sources.title: Aristotle, section 1: Aristotle's Life

sources.geography: Stagira, Athens, Assos, Lesbos, Macedon and Chalcis
sources.summary: Reconstructs Aristotle's movements, the invitation to teach Alexander in 343 BCE and his return to Athens to establish the Lyceum in 335 BCE.
sources.limitations: The duration and substance of Alexander's tuition are uncertain. It provides no basis for placing Aristotle in Alexandria. A player's visit, lesson, dialogue or scholarly recognition is fictional and needs an explicit journey to the appropriate place and a compatible date.

sources.title: Euclid of Alexandria: biography and evidence

sources.geography: Alexandria, Egypt

sources.limitations: His precise birth, death, birthplace and career chronology are uncertain. Circa 300 BCE is an approximate scholarly setting, not an exact publication or appointment date. Anecdotes and a player's personal encounter must not be represented as verified biographical incidents.

sources.title: Intellectual Pursuits of the Hellenistic Age

sources.limitations: It does not establish an exact foundation year or prove that particular careers were available before the institutions developed. The game uses an approximate early-third-century opening for its institution-specific opportunities. Later scholars discussed in the overview require their own chronological guards.

sources.title: Reconstructions: The Pharos of Alexandria
sources.publisher: Alexandria and Mediterranean Research Center, Bibliotheca Alexandrina
sources.period: Pharos erection during 283–279 BCE under Ptolemy II; later monuments have separate dates
sources.geography: Alexandria and its Mediterranean coast
sources.summary: Dates the lighthouse to the reign of Ptolemy II, between 283 and 279 BCE, and explains the use of archaeological and historical evidence in modern reconstructions.
sources.limitations: A reconstruction overview, not a fully recovered original building. A completed lighthouse must not appear at the 350 BCE birth or 331 BCE city foundation. Pharos Island existed earlier; its name alone need not imply the lighthouse. The page's Ptolemy III Serapeum belongs after this cohort's age-100 record.

It does not establish the game's household frequencies, starting cash, ability ranges, care arrangements or fictional family outcomes. Later Ptolemaic institutions must not be assumed at birth.

economy.description: Household accounts use drachmas (dr). Net worth includes cash and the estimated sale value of possessions, less debt. Unpaid unavoidable costs can become debt. Amounts are fixed game values, not reconstructed historical prices or wages. There is no modern-currency conversion or automatic interest. The same simplified accounting unit is used across this lifetime's changes of ruler; it does not imply a fixed exchange rate or uniform historical coinage. A voluntarily accepted moneylender loan has its own balance and deadline. Ordinary household debt keeps automatic repayment; this loan must be paid deliberately. Its upfront charge and optional extension charge are fixed game terms, not measured ancient prices. Collectors pursue only that accepted loan.

assets.title: Tool chest
assets.description: Unlocks hinge, strap and fitting repairs at Tool handling 15. Sell for 30 drachmas.

assets.title: Workshop share
assets.description: Earn 10 drachmas each year you survive. Sell for 120 drachmas.

health.description: Early life keeps the easier health rules. From age 18, serious illness episodes use the full age-specific baseline from a Roman Egyptian female life-table comparison. Illness appears, Health falls and a care choice interrupts time before the condition can become fatal. Current Health, care and household support can change the outcome; dangerous choices retain their stated risks. Exact mortality for the Egyptian coast in this era is unknown. The later Roman comparison is an estimate for the setting, not a measured rate for this character. Disease selection, severity and care effects are authored game rules.

relationships.description: Friends, business partners and romantic relationships are explicit ties with people actually met in this life. Friendship and shared work can coexist with a love interest or spouse. Contact, conflict and neglect affect closeness. Ending one role leaves the others intact. Only the existing close household-care rules affect recovery; friends and business partners create no automatic income or extra health bonus. These arrangements and numeric rewards are fictional gameplay.

knowledge.description: Knowledge needs continued use. From age 12, two full years without a recorded learning gain lead to a loss of 1 point per year. Lessons, research, work and events with positive Knowledge effects refresh practice, including at the stat cap. Ageing also reduces Knowledge by 0.5 per year from 50, 1 from 65 and 1.5 from 80. These are authored game rules, not measured cognitive ageing rates. Skill proficiencies are separate.

routes.title: Sculpture
routes.description: Carve a figure for a household, then take on work that other makers come to inspect.

routes.title: Philosophy
routes.description: Test an argument in conversation and teach it well enough for a pupil to question you.

routes.title: Seafaring
routes.description: Bring a cargo to its landing, keep a clear account and earn another place aboard.

routes.title: Military
routes.description: Account for stores, carry out a unit's orders and seek recognition for completed service.

routes.title: Commerce
routes.description: Fill an order, settle the supplier's account and persuade a customer to return.

routes.title: Astronomy & Calendar Tables
routes.description: Compare observations, correct the columns and prepare tables another reader can check.

routes.title: Music & Performance
routes.description: Learn the entrances, finish an engagement and give a host a reason to invite the ensemble back.

routes.title: Service
routes.description: Bring the army's grain through on the supply road and have your lead entered in the unit's record.

routes.title: Benefactor
routes.description: Pay for a well, granary, school or healing house the village needs, then for a second work the district relies on.

routes.title: Alexander the Great: work and legacy
routes.description: Enter through campaign service while Alexander is in Egypt. Logistics, command and a completed strategic operation matter; an age-28 General appointment is not an entry requirement.

routes.title: Aristotle: work and legacy
routes.description: Start with argument and observation at the Lyceum, then build reviewed inquiry and teaching. Later work continues through the Aristotelian school and makes no claim of a dead teacher's personal endorsement.

routes.title: Euclid: work and legacy
routes.description: Join the geometrical tradition associated with the Elements around 300 BCE. The path rewards justified constructions and a coherent deductive collection, without inventing a Museum appointment or a precise death date.

routes.title: Lysippos: work and legacy
routes.description: Develop measured models, portrait proportions and bronze workshop projects. Stone sculpture is useful training, but cannot alone establish Lysippos's distinctive bronze achievement.

routes.title: Pytheas of Massalia: work and legacy
routes.description: Prepare an expedition, collect navigational observations and deliver a checked voyage account. The route preserves uncertainty about the lost work and the identity of Thule.

routes.title: Menander: work and legacy
routes.description: Write, revise, rehearse and stage comedy about human situations. Political office and scientific mastery do not substitute for dramatic achievement.

routes.title: Demetrius the Besieger: work and legacy
routes.description: An authored service encounter after the Gaza campaign leaves enough years to prepare real siege works. Machinery and a negotiated settlement remain Epic; only successful alternate-history capture of Rhodes supports Legendary.

stages.title: Epic contribution after a Legendary outcome

routes.title: Theophrastus: work and legacy
routes.description: Treat Aristotle's colleague and successor as an investigator in his own right. Comparative plant observations, seasons and a reviewed botanical account define the route.

routes.title: Zeno of Citium: work and legacy
routes.description: Develop argument, ethical inquiry and public teaching. Zeno remains Epic unless an independently functioning Stoic school is actually established through a separate funded programme.

stages.title: Epic contribution after a Legendary outcome

routes.title: Ptolemy I Soter: work and legacy
routes.description: Build audited administration, supply and political support before attempting a durable independent hereditary government. Becoming satrap, gaining wealth or reaching 305 BCE does not found a dynasty by itself.

stages.title: Epic contribution after a Legendary outcome

routes.title: Cleomenes of Naucratis: work and legacy
routes.description: Develop actual grain accounts, deliveries and revenue oversight. Ancient accounts of Cleomenes are hostile; humane relief choices are authored alternatives, not a proven benevolent historical policy.

achievements.title: A customer's sculpture
achievements.description: Philista keeps the finished figure. Menon names you as its maker when a visitor asks who carved it.

achievements.title: A distinguished relief
achievements.description: The procession relief passes Menon's inspection. Philista accepts the commission, and younger workers come to examine the cuts.

achievements.title: A remembered argument
achievements.description: Kleio can explain your argument about agreements in her own words. Apollonios keeps the checked outline for another lesson.

achievements.title: A teaching circle
achievements.description: Kleio and Apollonios return with objections to your collected discussions. The revised text becomes the basis of regular meetings.

achievements.title: A completed cargo voyage
achievements.description: Tasos signs for the cargo at the landing. Nikeratos keeps your name beside the completed delivery.

achievements.title: A trusted difficult passage
achievements.description: Crew and cargo reach the quay after a difficult passage. Nikeratos recommends you for a task with greater responsibility.

achievements.title: A recorded service assignment
achievements.description: Dion and Herakleides check the unit's stores against your record and enter your name beside the completed assignment.

achievements.title: A service distinction
achievements.description: Dion and Herakleides record your handling of a difficult unit assignment. Their commendation can support an application for further responsibility.

achievements.title: A fulfilled customer order
achievements.description: Berenike accepts the delivered order. Sarapion is paid, and your copy of the account shows the sum you kept.

achievements.title: A repeat supply agreement
achievements.description: Sarapion and Berenike agree to repeat the arrangement. Your seal identifies the orders placed through the venture.

achievements.title: A corrected seasonal table
achievements.description: Heron checks your arithmetic. Isidora keeps the corrected seasonal table, including the distinction between calculated entries and uncertain expectations.

achievements.title: A credited table collection
achievements.description: Heron and Isidora credit the corrections in your compared tables. Your notes show how each calculation was checked and where uncertainty remains.

achievements.title: A paid musical engagement
achievements.description: Melitta performs beside you at Theon's gathering. The agreed programme is finished, and the household pays for the engagement.

achievements.title: A distinguished repeat invitation
achievements.description: Your signals keep the ensemble together through its programme. Theon credits your organisation and commissions another engagement.

achievements.title: Convoy distinction
achievements.description: Dion records that you led an escort of army grain through a dangerous road and brought it in.

achievements.title: A work for the village
achievements.description: Harpocras cuts your name into the dedication stone. Thaesis tells her children who paid for the work.

achievements.title: Benefactor of the district
achievements.description: Heraclides enters two public works under your name in the district register.

achievements.title: Entered Alexander the Great's working circle
achievements.description: An authored encounter and working introduction at Egypt, then the Macedonian campaign train. This is access to work, not a contribution rank or the figure's special title.
